system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2142-11-07 04:58:00 to 2142-11-09 19:27:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, bilateral below-knee amputations, and a history of multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections was admitted with fevers to 103 and chills. She was found to have a urinary tract infection caused by carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae, which was treated with intravenous meropenem after initial broad-spectrum coverage. A PICC line was placed for outpatient antibiotic completion. During admission, stool was noted in the vaginal vault, prompting evaluation for a rectovaginal fistula; however, MRI and colonoscopy showed no fistula or mass. Left stump infection was assessed with ultrasound, which showed no abscess, and vascular surgery recommended outpatient follow-up. Acute kidney injury was monitored, with creatinine fluctuating but ultimately improving to 1.4. The patient was discharged home on oral vancomycin for C. diff prophylaxis, with follow-up planned in colorectal, vascular, and gynecology clinics.
problems: Urinary tract infection, site not specified
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

There is linear opacity at the right apex, unchanged, compatible with scar. 
The heart size is unchanged, top normal and likely exaggerated by AP
technique.  There is no pneumothorax or effusion.  There is mild prominence of
the pulmonary vasculature, without frank edema.  An IVC filter is noted in the
abdomen.

frontal view likely reflect atelectasis given low lung volumes.  Repeat

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. You're in the emergency department. Can you tell me what brought you in tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I started feeling really sick—nauseous, vomiting, and I had a fever. It came on fast, maybe an hour ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any belly pain, diarrhea, or trouble breathing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no belly pain or diarrhea. Just the nausea and fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rate was very high when you arrived, and your blood pressure dropped. We also saw signs of high potassium on your EKG. We gave you some meds to stabilize that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High potassium? I didn’t know that was an issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common when the kidneys aren’t working well, especially during an infection. We’ve treated it, and your levels are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So what’s going on? Why did I crash like this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We think you had a urinary tract infection that turned into sepsis. Your urine showed a lot of bacteria and white blood cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I’ve had these before. They’re always tough to treat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and because of your history, we started strong antibiotics—Vancomycin, Zosyn, and Levofloxacin—to cover resistant bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they work? Last time it was Klebsiella, and it was resistant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. We’ve sent your urine for culture to see exactly what we’re dealing with.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidneys? My creatinine was high last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is elevated at 2.4, but we think it’s from low blood pressure and dehydration. We’re giving fluids, and it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m just worried about another long stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re moving fast. You’re being admitted to the MICU for close monitoring tonight. We’ll reassess in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. We placed a central line this morning to make giving antibiotics and fluids easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my arm feels tight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the dressing. It should feel better soon. No complications—we checked with an X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Any news on the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still pending, but we’re staying ahead of it. We switched from Zosyn to doripenem because of your past resistant infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds familiar. Is it stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s broader and better for ESBL-type bacteria, which we suspect based on your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your urine culture came back. It’s Klebsiella pneumoniae, but this time it’s sensitive to ciprofloxacin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So can I stop the IV antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll switch you to oral ciprofloxacin. You’ll take it twice a day for 10 days total, including after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can lower blood sugar, so monitor closely. Take it with food, but not with milk or calcium supplements—wait four hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my kidneys? How are they doing?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Creatinine is down to 1.7 from 2.4. That’s a good sign your kidneys are recovering with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my blood pressure? It’s usually high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave one dose of lisinopril today. We’re not restarting it now—your PCP will decide if you need it once your kidney function stabilizes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my stump? It’s been sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked—no signs of infection. It’s a pressure sore, so keep using the cushion and change position often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. You’re off IV meds, and your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the ciprofloxacin, keep the central line dressing on for one week, and follow up with your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I was on Lantus 5 units.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to your home regimen—Lantus 5 units twice daily and Humalog as needed. Watch for low sugars with the cipro.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You responded well. We’re glad you’re on the mend. A nurse will go over your discharge papers now.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, bilateral below-knee amputations, and a history of multidrug-resistant urinary tract infections presented with nausea, vomiting, and fever. She developed septic shock with hypotension and hyperkalemia, requiring ICU admission. Initial broad-spectrum antibiotics were given, later de-escalated to ciprofloxacin after urine culture identified Klebsiella pneumoniae sensitive to ciprofloxacin. Her acute kidney injury, attributed to pre-renal causes from hypovolemia, improved with intravenous fluids. A central line was placed for antibiotic access and later removed. She was discharged home on oral ciprofloxacin with stable vital signs and improved renal function, with follow-up planned with her primary care provider.
